fact_1: A malignant tumor made of myoepithelial cells. In the salivary glands the diagnosis requires a tumor that is unequivocally malignant and exclusively myoepithelial. Older papers call it malignant myoepithelioma.
fact_2: About 0.013 per 100,000 person-years, from 368 patients in the U.S. SEER registry, 1973 to 2012. The U.S. National Cancer Database recorded 336 cases from 2004 to 2020.
fact_3: In 691 patients pooled from the published literature, the major salivary glands were the most common site (36.4%), followed by minor salivary glands, skin and soft tissue, and breast.
fact_4: In the National Cancer Database, survival was 79.4% at two years, 66.5% at five and 52.0% at ten, across all sites. The pooled literature gives a median overall survival of 167 months. Outcomes differ sharply by site, grade and age.
fact_5: Surgery. Complete removal with clear margins was associated with better progression-free and overall survival in the pooled analysis. There are no established standards for drug treatment.
fact_6: Largely a disease of gene fusions. EWSR1 is rearranged in 45% of myoepithelial tumors outside the salivary glands, and 70% of salivary cases carry a fusion, most involving PLAG1.
fact_8: Epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma, which is a separate diagnosis, and myoepithelioma, which is the benign counterpart.
fact_9: cureMEC: The Myoepithelial Carcinoma Project, a patient-driven research initiative launched in 2022.

not_advice: This is a summary of published research, compiled by a patient. It is not medical advice.
numbers: In the U.S. National Cancer Database (336 patients, all body sites), 79.4% were alive at 2 years, 66.5% at 5 years and 52.0% at 10 years. In 691 patients pooled from the published literature, median overall survival was 167 months, about 14 years. These are group figures and do not predict one person's course.
own: Your doctors treat the disease, but you have to run the project. With a disease this rare, many of the people treating you may be seeing it for the first time. Arrive prepared, ask until you understand, and keep your own records.
plan_1: Ask for the full written report. Find three things on it: the exact diagnosis line, the stains that were positive, and what it says about the margin. Peter’s read “adnexal carcinoma, consistent with myoepithelial carcinoma,” with invasion close to the margin.
plan_1_title: Get the pathology report in your hands
plan_2: Ask for a second pathology opinion at a center that sees these tumors. In one series most cases had first been given a different diagnosis. Peter’s diagnosis came from a second-opinion review.
plan_2_title: Get the slides read a second time
plan_3: Ask whether the tumor has been tested for gene fusions such as EWSR1 and PLAG1, and for INI1. The result affects how the tumor is classified and what is known about how it behaves.
plan_4: Ask each doctor how many cases they have treated. The published series come from specialist units: a sarcoma unit for soft-tissue disease, tertiary cancer centers for salivary disease. Ask for your case to go to a tumor board.
plan_4_title: Find a team that has seen it
plan_5: Ask which scans are needed to look for spread, and keep copies of the images and the reports. PET, CT and MRI were ordered for Peter.
plan_6: Complete removal with clear margins was associated with better survival in the pooled data. Ask whether the margin was clear, what happens if it was not, and whether radiotherapy afterward is worth discussing.
plan_6_title: Talk about margins, before surgery and after
plan_7: The authors of the adult soft-tissue series say trial enrollment should be encouraged. Ask whether your tissue can be banked for research. cureMEC is building biospecimen collections, and Peter donates his.
plan_7_title: Ask about trials, and about your tissue
plan_8: This disease returns often. In a 101-tumor soft-tissue series, 42% of malignant tumors recurred, and follow-up ran as long as 21 years. Agree how often you will be checked, and do not let it slide when you feel well.
plan_8_title: Set a surveillance schedule and keep it
